item.content:encoded:
By NOAH TRISTER AP Baseball Writer
Justin Verlander and Max Scherzer were together on some memorable Detroit teams before moving on and winning championships elsewhere.
Will they eventually enter the Hall of Fame as part of the same class?
The first question is whether both will retire after this season. The 43-year-old Verlander has already announced this is his final year. He’s made only one start in a reunion season with the Tigers, although Detroit fans are hoping he can return for another this coming week.
Scherzer’s future is less clear. The 42-year-old right-hander is slated to start Tuesday at Baltimore as the Blue Jays try to keep their flickering playoff hopes alive, but Scherzer has posted ERAs over 5.00 both this season and last. He’s on a one-year contract with Toronto.
Some other prominent players may also have made — or might be making — their last appearances in the major leagues. Trey Mancini signed a one-day contract to retire with the Orioles and was celebrated this past weekend in Baltimore. Andrew McCutchen and Carlos Santana, both 39, were released last month. Craig Kimbrel, now 38, has pitched for 10 different big league teams in the last six seasons.
Paul Goldschmidt is 39, but his team — the New York Yankees — is heading to the playoffs. And he may be more important than expected if Aaron Judge is out.
With a lockout possible after this season, there could be some retirements we don’t anticipate. Rick Sutcliffe, Bo Jackson and Hall of Famer Goose Gossage, for example, never played again after the 1994 strike but didn’t actually retire until the following year.
Trivia time
Who is the most recent player voted into the Hall of Fame by the BBWAA whose primary team was the Tigers? (The drought is likely to end soon with Miguel Cabrera and then Verlander.)
Performance of the week
Angel Martínez homered from both sides of the plate and had four hits in Cleveland’s 12-6 win over the Athletics on Saturday night. The Guardians have won five straight and are closing in on a postseason spot. They have a one-game lead over the Chicago White Sox atop the AL Central, and it’s another three games back from the White Sox to Toronto and Houston in the race for the last wild card.
In the National League, Philadelphia leads Arizona by four games for the final wild card, so anyone rooting for chaos this coming week may be disappointed.
Comeback of the week
Detroit was down 8-2 in the fifth inning Friday night before scoring nine unanswered runs to win 11-8 over the White Sox. Kevin McGonigle hit a three-run triple, and both Hao-Yu Lee and Riley Greene added two-run homers during the comeback. Detroit’s win probability was down to 3.2% in the fourth inning according to Baseball Savant.
That’s the only game the Tigers have won out of their last five. They’ve been eliminated from the playoff race, the end of a frustrating season in which nothing seemed to go as planned.
Team of the week
The Los Angeles Dodgers and San Diego Padres both went 6-1, with the Dodgers posting the superior run differential. A three-game sweep of San Francisco leaves the Dodgers four games ahead of Atlanta for the second bye in the National League as they try for a third consecutive World Series title.
There are still health concerns for the Dodgers, with Shohei Ohtani on the injured list and Blake Snell having left his last start after one inning.
Los Angeles did get Edwin Diaz back, and he threw scoreless innings on back-to-back days Friday and Saturday.
Trivia answer
Al Kaline, who was inducted in 1980.
George Kell, Hal Newhouser, Jim Bunning, Sparky Anderson, Jack Morris and Alan Trammell have been elected since then with the Tigers as their primary team, but they weren’t voted in by the BBWAA.

item.title: [FanGraphs] Bobby Witt Jr. and the Off-Peak MVP Season
item.dc:creator: Davy Andrews
item.description: Bobby Witt Jr. is having a down year. He’s running his worst batting line in three seasons. He’s in danger of missing the 20-homer threshold for the first time in his career. A lower back injury in July will also limit him to a career low in games played. Put it together, and Witt is on pace to put up his the lowest WAR total since his 5.9-win 2023 campaign. item.content:encoded:
Bobby Witt Jr. is having a down year. He’s running his worst batting line in three seasons. He’s in danger of missing the 20-homer threshold for the first time in his career. A lower back injury in July will also limit him to a career low in games played. Put it together, and Witt is on pace to put up his the lowest WAR total since his 5.9-win 2023 campaign. Oh, and he also grabbed hold of the American League lead in WAR back in July and still hasn’t relinquished it. A down year by Bobby Witt Jr.’s standards is still good enough to make him a deserving MVP.
I don’t know if Witt is going to win his first MVP this year. Ours is the only flavor of WAR in which he leads the AL, and he leads by just a quarter of a win. He ranks third by Baseball Reference’s rWAR and is eighth by Baseball Prospectus’ WARP. Yordan Alvarez leads all of baseball in WARP because he’s hitting like, well, Yordan Alvarez and staying healthy like, well, someone other than Yordan Alvarez. Cam Schlittler leads the AL in Baseball Reference WAR, and he’s been so dominant that he deserves consideration for the Cy Young-MVP combo — if only he’d pitched just 23 fewer innings last year, he could’ve gone for the trifecta with Rookie of the Year. Kevin McGonigle has played like an MVP from the moment he arrived in Detroit, and Junior Caminero has surpassed 40 home runs for the second season in a row as a 23-year-old. All of these guys have a case, and they aren’t the only ones who merit inclusion in the discussion:
| Name | fWAR Rk | fWAR | rWAR Rk | rWAR | WARP Rk | WARP | Avg Rk | Avg WAR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bobby Witt Jr. | 1 | 6.6 | 3 | 6.5 | 8 | 5 | 4 | 6.0 |
| Yordan Alvarez | 2 | 6.4 | 4 | 6.4 | 1 | 7.3 | 2 | 6.7 |
| Cam Schlittler | 3 | 6.1 | 1 | 7 | 3 | 5.8 | 2 | 6.3 |
| Dylan Cease | 4 | 5.5 | 8 | 5.7 | 12 | 4.6 | 8 | 5.3 |
| Miguel Vargas | 5 | 5.2 | 10 | 5.3 | 2 | 5.9 | 6 | 5.5 |
| Junior Caminero | 6 | 5.2 | 7 | 5.7 | 5 | 5.3 | 6 | 5.4 |
| Kevin McGonigle | 7 | 5.1 | 2 | 6.7 | 4 | 5.3 | 4 | 5.7 |
| Randy Arozarena | 8 | 5.1 | 11 | 5.3 | 16 | 4 | 12 | 4.8 |
| Dillon Dingler | 9 | 4.6 | 25 | 4 | 23 | 3.3 | 19 | 4.0 |
| Drew Rasmussen | 10 | 4.6 | 21 | 4.2 | 13 | 4.4 | 15 | 4.4 |
| Reid Detmers | 11 | 4.6 | 35 | 3.7 | 11 | 4.7 | 19 | 4.3 |
| Parker Messick | 13 | 4.6 | 6 | 5.8 | 9 | 4.8 | 9 | 5.1 |
| Pete Alonso | 14 | 4.2 | 18 | 4.3 | 6 | 5.3 | 13 | 4.6 |
| Ceddanne Rafaela | 21 | 3.9 | 9 | 5.4 | 94 | 1.7 | 41 | 3.7 |
| Gavin Williams | 27 | 3.7 | 46 | 3.1 | 7 | 5.2 | 27 | 4.0 |
| Wilyer Abreu | 32 | 3.4 | 5 | 5.8 | 20 | 3.6 | 19 | 4.3 |
| Mike Trout | 40 | 3.2 | 28 | 3.9 | 10 | 4.8 | 26 | 4.0 |
Pete Crow-Armstrong, Jacob Misiorowski, Schlittler, McGonigle and JJ Wetherholt have made the AL MVP the only major award that’s really in question). If you want to read a particularly good example, you should check out the one Mario Delgado Genzor wrote for Baseball Prospectus on Friday. I want to focus on something slightly different — namely, how good Witt has already been in years when he missed out on an MVP and how unusual it would be for him to win it this year.
(A quick note before we get into it: We’re about to spend a lot of time talking about WAR. I know I mentioned rWAR and WARP earlier. They’re an important piece of the puzzle, especially due to the outsized effect rWAR in particular has on the MVP conversation, but from here on out, we’re sticking with good old FanGraphs WAR.)
This is Witt’s fifth major league season, and you could argue that it’s his fourth consecutive MVP-caliber campaign. Mind you, that argument would focus only on 2022, in which he put up 5.9 WAR, good for 10th in the majors. There’s no argument to be had about the 2024 and 2025 seasons. That said, along with Shohei Ohtani’s combined 9.2-WAR 2022 sesaon, they are the two most valuable seasons this decade for which a position player did not win an MVP. In 2024, Witt ran a 169 wRC+, stole 31 bases, and put up a Fielding Run Value of 11, fourth among all shortstops. That was good for 10.5 WAR, and it took the best season of Aaron Judge’s career – 58 home runs, a 19% walk rate, and a .322 batting average – to beat him. In 2025, Witt put up 8.0 WAR with a 130 wRC+, 38 steals, and 20 FRV, the best mark among all shortstops. Again, he was bested by a 10-win season from Judge and Cal Raleigh’s 60-homer campaign. Witt has never received a first place MVP vote.
Crow-Armstrong, who has the National League MVP all but locked down, gives us a great example of what it normally takes to win an MVP award. He may even finish with 10.5 WAR through his excellence in all three phases of the game, just like Witt did in 2024. Players like Judge, Ohtani, and Mike Trout, whose base level of talent is so high that a healthy campaign is almost sure to keep them a step above the rest of the league, don’t come around all that often. Even when they do come around, they still need to be playing at something close to their peak, and peaks don’t last that long. Until Ohtani, the only player to win more than three MVPs was Barry Bonds, whose regimen for raising and widening his peak has been well documented. Sometimes that’s because of voter fatigue, but often it’s because somebody else popped up with an amazing, undeniable season like PCA’s. Most of the time, the MVP is an already great player for whom everything goes perfectly. They stay healthy and they play not just their best, but over their heads. Think of Ronald Acuña Jr. winning the NL MVP in 2023 with 9.1 WAR, 4.1 more than his next-best total, or Mookie Betts winning the AL MVP in 2018 with 10.2 WAR, 2.8 more than his next-best total.
Generally speaking, since the voting started getting more rigorous in the last couple decades, those are the two categories of players who win MVPs. We see all-time greats who perform like only they are capable of performing, and we see excellent players who put it all together in a blaze of glory. Witt’s 2024 season probably falls into that second category. He wasn’t quite at his defensive or baserunning peak, but he put up his best season at the plate by nearly 40 points of wRC+ and DRC+, and he ended up with an all-timer of a season. His 10.5 WAR tied for the 36th-best position player campaign of all time. His company? Willie Mays and Babe Ruth twice apiece, Barry Bonds, and Rogers Hornsby. Unfortunately, he ran into one of those special players from the first category, in the form of Judge. If Witt had put up those 2024 numbers this year, he’d be en route to a unanimous MVP just like PCA.
But I said “in theory” earlier, and I said it because Witt isn’t done yet. He’s still just 26, and if not for those weeks he missed with back tightness, or a wOBA that’s more than 30 points below his xwOBA, he’d now be wrapping up his third straight seven-plus-win season. He’s elite in every facet of the game and he doesn’t look like he’s in danger of slowing down any time soon. It wouldn’t be much of a shock to see him rediscover his nine- or 10-win form. In other words, there’s at least a chance Witt belongs to that first category of player and not the second.
Earlier I mentioned Acuña and Betts claiming MVPs by putting up the best years of their careers by a long shot. That’s pretty standard. Especially in recent years, it’s awfully rare for a player to take home an MVP award in something other than the best season of their career, unless they also won the MVP in the best year of their career. Leaving those multi-time MVPs out (and excluding 2020 for obvious reasons), here’s the whole list of players who won an MVP in a year that wasn’t their best by fWAR since 2011: Giancarlo Stanton and Paul Goldschmidt.
Goldschmidt put up 6.8 WAR in his 2022 NL MVP season and 7.2 in 2015. In that sense, Goldschmidt fit a third archetype: the established star who doesn’t put up their biggest WAR total, and instead wins MVP as something of a career achievement award. Stanton put up 6.5 WAR in 2017, not quite the 6.8-win campaign he put up in 2014, but he was facing a weaker field, he was more established as a star, and he had the cachet of a 59-homer season. We’re talking about gaps of less than half a win. We had some multi-time winners, but Acuña, Betts, Cody Bellinger, Christian Yelich, Jose Altuve, Kris Bryant, Josh Donaldson, Andrew McCutchen, and Buster Posey all won MVP in the best seasons of their career by fWAR.
Let’s say that Witt does win the MVP this year. For the sake of round numbers, let’s say he closes strong and finishes with 7.0 WAR. That would be just the third-best season of his career, and a full 3.5 WAR below his career-high. Baseball Reference lists MVP winners going back to 1911, and in that time, Witt would become just the ninth position player to win MVP in a season that trailed their best year by such a wide margin. The list of players to do it before him is full of three-time MVPs like Joe DiMaggio, Mickey Mantle, and Mike Schmidt. Not only that, but you’ll note that if Witt does make this list, the only higher number in either column will belong to Mantle:
| Player | MVP Year | MVP WAR | Best Year | Best WAR | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frankie Frisch | 1931 | 4.1 | 1927 | 9.7 | 5.6 |
| Mickey Mantle | 1962 | 6.0 | 1956 | 11.5 | 5.5 |
| Willie Stargell | 1979 | 2.7 | 1971 | 8.2 | 5.4 |
| Joe DiMaggio | 1947 | 4.8 | 1941 | 9.7 | 4.9 |
| Freddie Freeman | 2020* | 3.0 | 2023 | 7.7 | 4.7 |
| Robin Yount | 1989 | 5.3 | 1982 | 9.8 | 4.5 |
| Andre Dawson | 1987 | 3.5 | 1982 | 7.3 | 3.8 |
| Mike Schmidt | 1986 | 5.8 | 1974 | 9.4 | 3.6 |
| Roger Peckinpaugh | 1925 | 2.4 | 1919 | 5.9 | 3.5 |
The last person to do so was Robin Yount, who won the AL MVP with 9.8 WAR in 1982, and then again with 5.3 WAR in 1989, long before anybody knew that Total Zone considered him the 11th-worst defender in the majors. This hasn’t happened in nearly 30 years, and Witt is in a very different boat here. He’s not one of the two MVP favorites because his season looks great to the eye but doesn’t fool the advanced metrics. He’s not an aging star who can count on some lifetime-achievement votes. He’s a young gun who’s leading his league in WAR because he excels in every facet of the game.
I realize that this is far from the most meticulous analysis I’ve ever conducted, and that MVP voting is and should be about more than WAR. Still, I hope I’ve put this season in the context it deserves. By our measuring stick, Witt has been the best player in the American League this season. He’s done so despite missing time due to injury. He’s done so despite some bad batted ball luck. And he’s done so despite not even coming close to the highest gear we know he’s got available to him, because that gear is so high that it’s normally reserved for inner-circle Hall of Famers. However the voting goes, Witt’s been in MVP form for three or four years now.
Davy Andrews is a Brooklyn-based musician and a writer at FanGraphs. He can be found on Bluesky @davyandrewsdavy.bsky.social.

item.content:encoded:
The Mets have just nine games left in the season, and all of the attention is already shifting to the 2027 campaign. There are a lot of questions that the Mets have to answer this winter, and seeing the fans' over-the-top reaction to Pete Alonso's return this week shows how much work the front office needs to do to win back the trust of its fan base.
The free agent market is a bit thin this year, but it does have a few players who could help the Mets bolster their roster, particularly in the pitching department. That tally doesn't include Bo Bichette, whose opt-out decision will also play a significant role in how much money President of Baseball Operations David Stearns has to work with in free agency.
That said, let's dive into five potential free agents that the Mets should pursue this winter.
1. LHP Tarik Skubal
We took a deeper dive into the Tarik Skubal fit for the Mets last week, but it is fair to wonder if the fans' vitriolic display at Citi Field this week may inspire Steve Cohen to go for the top pitcher on the board as a make-good to them.
There are certainly injury risks with Skubal, but there isn't a better pitcher on the board, and his arrival would push the rest of the current rotation into more appropriate roles, starting with Nolan McLean as one of the best No. 2's in baseball.
2. LHP Robbie Ray
Skubal alone would bolster the Mets' rotation but Stearns should also look to add a veteran for the middle of the rotation who can give them quality innings. Enter Robbie Ray, a former Cy Young winner who is 13-8 with a 3.60 ERA in 30 appearances (including 29 starts) between the Giants and Padres.
The Mets would get a veteran lefty who has thrown at least 162.2 innings in four of the past six seasons, with the only exceptions being the 2022 and 2023 campaigns when he missed significant time rehabbing from Tommy John surgery. Putting Ray as the Mets' third starter would allow Stearns to bump Christian Scott down to the No. 4 spot and have healthy competition for the fifth between Sean Manaea, Jonah Tong, Zac Thornton and a slew of other depth options.
3. 1B/3B Alec Bohm
First base is one of the bigger questions on the Mets' roster, and they can't go into next season hoping that the combination of Jared Young, Mark Vientos, Brett Baty and Jorge Polanco can solve it. One good fit here could be Alec Bohm, who is hitting .251 with 15 home runs, 84 RBIs and a .707 OPS in 534 at-bats for the Phillies.
If the Mets feel like Young can be part of a first base platoon, then Bohm would make sense as a partner since he is very strong against lefties, batting .293 with seven homers, 36 RBIs and an .828 OPS against them in 179 at-bats. Veteran Paul Goldschmidt could also fill a platoon role with Young, but the Mets would be better served going with someone in his prime as opposed to a Goldschmidt-type towards the end of his career.
Bohm's ability to play both infield corners could also be helpful in the event Bichette opts out.
4. OF Ramon Laureano
The Mets' decision to move on from Tyrone Taylor (via trade) and Luis Robert Jr. (via waivers) has left them with an all-left-handed-hitting outfield of Juan Soto, A.J. Ewing and Carson Benge. While all three are capable starters, it would make sense to add a veteran option who can hit right-handed since Nick Morabito appears to need more minor league seasoning to be ready for that fourth outfielder role.
A good buy-low fit here could be Ramón Laureano, who has missed most of the season after undergoing surgery to repair a torn labrum in his right hip in May. Laureano can play both outfield corners and is just a year removed from a solid 2025 campaign where he hit .281 with 24 homers, 76 RBIs and an .855 OPS, so adding him on a one-year prove-it deal could give the Mets more flexibility to protect Juan Soto's health with DH days or sit one of Ewing or Benge against tough lefties.
5. RHP Evan Phillips
The Mets bullpen's strong performance post-deadline has lessened their need to go big-game hunting at the back end of the unit, but they still need to add a proven setup reliever to their mix. One name who could offer good value is Evan Phillips, who has pitched to a 3.68 ERA and 1.23 WHIP in 27 appearances for the Dodgers this season.
Phillips missed time with injuries this year but does have closing experience with Los Angeles, which could be valuable if Devin Williams struggles in his second year with the Mets. The injury issues Phillips had may drive his price down to a one- or two-year contract, which would be right up Stearns' wheelhouse and make him a good complement to the likes of Williams, Kodai Senga, Reed Garrett and Daniel Duarte in the relief mix.

Mike Phillips is a contributor to the Mets On SI site. Mike has been covering the Mets since 2011 for various websites, including Metstradamus and Kiners Korner. Mike has a Masters Degree from Iona University in Sports Communications and Media and also has experience covering the NFL and college basketball on FanSided. item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees first baseman Paul Goldschmidt has flipped the script.
The addition of Luis Garcia Jr. had completely clouded Goldschmidt's role, and it appeared that the impending returns of Aaron Judge and Giancarlo Stanton would make the former NL MVP rather disposable.
My, how things have changed.
Yes, Goldschmidt's at-bats have still been somewhat sparse since the arrival of Garcia at the MLB trade deadline, but with Judge and Stanton now both potentially out for the playoffs (or at least the Wild Card Series), Goldschmidt's value just increased exponentially.
Suddenly, Goldschmidt is now one of the Yankees' very best options against left-handed pitching, and he may get some starts in the playoffs now that Judge and Stanton are both on the shelf.
Goldschmidt has always mashed southpaws, owning a lifetime 1.006 OPS against them. This year, he is slashing .309/.404/.592 versus lefties, making him a must on New York's playoff squad.
It should also be noted that after a miserable month of July and after barely playing in August, Goldschmidt has gone 6-for-18 at the plate this month, so he is starting to rediscover his stroke as October draws near.
And with the Boston Red Sox — New York's likely Wild Card opponent — being loaded with left-handers, Goldschmidt will likely get significant playing time early on in the postseason.
In that scenario, Ben Rice would serve as the DH — a role that almost certainly would have gone to Stanton had he been available — and Goldschmidt will play over at first base. Garcia would then come off the bench as a pinch hitter against righties.
Goldschmidt's overall numbers this season look solid, as he is slashing .253/.316/.455 with 18 home runs and 50 RBI across 370 trips to the dish. Not bad for a 39-year-old.
Goldschmidt's production has nose dived since then, but he appears to be kicking it back into gear just in time for the playoffs.
And now that Judge and Stanton are both on the shelf, you can expect Goldschmidt to play a pivotal role.

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX -- The sound off the bat got an eruption of sound from the Chase Field crowd. But as the ball off the bat of Nolan Arenado traveled toward the left-foul pole, it began to hook. It ultimately slid foul, almost a go-ahead grand slam in the bottom of the fifth that would have kept the D-backs’ postseason chances alive.
One pitch later, Arenado hammered the next one fair into the left-field seats. Pendulum, swung.
It marked Arenado’s ninth career grand slam and third this year, tying Paul Goldschmidt (2013) and Eugenio Suárez (2025) for the most in a single season in franchise history. It was the turning point in the club’s 8-4 victory over the Yankees on Sunday during the 2026 regular-season home finale, marking their 47th comeback win of the year, the most in the Majors.
But with the Cubs (87-69), Padres (87-69) and Phillies (86-70) all winning on Sunday as well, the D-backs remain four games out of the third and final National League Wild Card spot with just six games to play. To paraphrase Yankees Hall of Famer Yogi Berra and one of his “Yogi-isms”:
“It’s getting late early.”
While the D-backs will conclude the regular season with a three-game series against San Diego next week, they trail the Padres by five games. That means Arizona will need to make up two games in the standings by the time it arrives at Petco Park next Friday to give themselves a chance at October baseball.
Regardless of what the next week holds for the 2026 D-backs as they embark on the road, what can’t be denied is that by virtue of their 45-37 record at Chase Field, they turned in the most successful season at home since 2017 (53-29).

item.content:encoded:
On Sunday, the New York Yankees will finish their series with the Arizona Diamondbacks.
The Yankees won the first game by a score of 9-2 (on Friday).
Paul Goldschmidt had one hit, one walk and two runs.
He was not in the lineup for Saturday’s 5-3 loss.
Goldschmidt also remains out of the lineup on Sunday.
7x MLB All-Star Will Be A Yankees Free Agent
With the season nearly over, it’s worth noting that Goldschmidt will become a free agent who is available to sign with any team in the MLB this winter.
He is being paid $4 million for the 2026 season.
If Goldschmidt wants to keep playing, it’s hard to imagine a world where the Yankees would not want him.
It’s also fair to wonder if any other teams would have interest.
In addition to being an incredible veteran in the clubhouse, the 39-year-old is still a very productive player.
Goldschmidt is batting .253 with 85 hits, 18 home runs, 50 RBIs, 44 runs and one stolen base in 102 games this year.
Looking At The Rest Of Goldschmidt’s Career
Goldschmidt was picked in the 8th round of the 2009 MLB Draft.
He spent the first eight years of his career with the Diamondbacks.
From 2013-18, Goldschmidt made five straight trips to the All-Star Game.
Following Arizona, Goldschmidt had another strong run with the St. Louis Cardinals (2019-24).
He made another trip to the All-Star Game (and won the 2022 National League MVP Award).
Looking At New York Right Now
The Yankees are the second-place team in the American League East with an 89-65 record in 154 games.
They have won seven out of their last ten games.

On Saturday, the New York Yankees will look to clinch a series victory when they play the second game of their series with the Diamondbacks in Arizona.
They won by a score of 9-2 on Friday night.
Paul Goldschmidt (who led off) had one hit, one walk and two runs.
Yankees Quickly Announce Paul Goldschmidt Change
For Saturday’s game, the Yankees have announced their starting lineup.
Underdog MLB wrote: “Yankees 9/19 B. Rice DH C. Bellinger LF L. García Jr. 1B H. Ramos RF G. Lombard Jr. SS A. Wells C A. Volpe 2B R. McMahon 3B J. Caballero CF C. Schlittler SP”
Goldschmidt has been removed from the lineup.
The seven-time All-Star is in the middle of his second season playing for New York.
He is currently batting .253 with 85 hits, 18 home runs, 50 RBIs, 44 runs and one stolen base in 102 games this year.
Goldschmidt had spent the first eight years of his career with Arizona.
In that span, he made six straight All-Star Games (2013-18).
Following the Diamondbacks, he had a six-year run with the St. Louis Cardinals that saw him win the 2022 National League MVP Award.
Looking At The Yankees On Saturday
The Yankees are the second-place team in the American League East with an 89-64 record in 153 games.
They are 8-2 over their last ten games.
Currently, the Yankees are 4.0 games back of the Tampa Bay Rays.
Looking At The D-Backs On Saturday
The Diamondbacks are the third-place team in the National League West with an 80-74 record in 154 games.
They are 4-6 over their last ten games.

As Guardians chase playoff spot, Jose Ramirez records career RBI 1,000
CLEVELAND — Cleveland’s baseball franchise has never had a player quite like Jose Ramirez.
Along with signing under-market contracts to remain with the Guardians twice and the many memorable moments in a Cleveland uniform over the past decade-plus, his assault on the record books added another chapter Sept. 18 in a 5-3 win over the Athletics, which allowed them to retake the lead in the American League Central race with eight game remaining.
In that win, Ramirez went 2-for-5 with a home run and two RBIs, which gave him 1,000 RBIs in his career. In doing so, he became the 12th active player to reach 1,000 RBIs, joining Freddie Freeman, Paul Goldschmidt, Manny Machado, Giancarlo Stanton, Mike Trout, Bryce Harper, Nolan Arenado, Andrew McCutchen, Salvador Perez, Eugenio Suarez and Carlos Santana.
“Very important to thank God for that opportunity to play here in this organization and to be bale to achieve that,” Ramirez said through a team translator. “But the most important part is that we’re able to win today because you guys know what I really want to do here, which is win.”
Jose Ramirez stats
He’s also just the second Cleveland player to hit that milestone with the franchise, joining Earl Averill (1,084), whose playing career ended in the early 1940s.
It’s a significant line on Ramirez's Hall of Fame resume. The home run also brought him within three of becoming only the ninth player in MLB history to reach the 300/300 club for home runs and stolen bases.
“I like to use round numbers,” Guardians manager Stephen Vogt said. “It’s 10 years of 100 RBIs. When you break it down that way, it’s incredible what he has accomplished, and he’s not even close to being done. And very few people get do it, and it’s really cool to be here to watch it.”
It was a milestone night for Ramirez, though it came at the end of what has been one of his more frustrating seasons, particularly over the last few weeks while he’s played through hamate been surgery rehab.
Jose Ramirez injury update
He’s posted a 90 wRC+, which would be the first time since he became a full-time player in 2016 he’s been below 100 (league average). Since he returned to the lineup on July 22, after the procedure, he’s hit .216 with a .567 OPS.
“I keep working on it every day,” Ramirez said. “I have to keep working in the training room every day because this type of injury is the type where one day you feel good, the next you don’t feel so well, but you have to keep grinding.”
Despite the lack of his usual MVP-caliber production on a nightly basis, Vogt and the Guardians have still applauded the way Ramirez has fought through the situation. It’s one of the attributes that often gets mentioned first when listing why they feel he’s so valuable to the organization.
“Even as he was coming back and we have to give him off days, he was not happy about it,” Vogt said. “He wants to play every day. He wants to give us everything that he has on any given day. We know that there’s days where he’s not feeling good and he still goes out and gives 100 percent of what he has that day.
“It’s such a great example for our young guys to see that just because you’re not feeling 100 percent, it doesn’t mean you can’t go out and compete and contribute to help the team win.”
Ryan Lewis covers the Guardians for the Beacon Journal. He can be reached at rlewis1@gannett.com.

item.content:encoded:
CLEVELAND -- As the Progressive Field crowd roared around him, José Ramírez paused and leaned back in the left-handed batter’s box to admire his work. There was no doubt where the baseball he launched to right field was headed.
That image has played on repeat over the past 14 seasons. This time, it came with a heavy dose of history, and it was well-timed as the Guardians continue to push for the postseason.
Ramírez tallied his 1,000th career RBI on Friday by launching his 297th career home run, in the sixth inning of the Guardians’ matchup with the A’s in the opener of a three-game series. The superstar third baseman joined Earl Averill (1,084) as the only players in Cleveland franchise history to hit the RBI milestone.
The Guardians improved to 79-75 with their third straight win. They entered Friday with the same record as the White Sox, but Chicago technically led the division because it holds the tiebreaker over Cleveland after winning the season series.
It means the Guardians must finish with more wins than the Sox to win the Central for a third straight year. Ramírez helped; his towering blast went a Statcast-projected 401 feet and had a 102.4 mph exit velocity.
Ramírez, who turned 34 years old on Thursday, is now just the 12th active player with 1,000 career RBIs, joining Freddie Freeman, Paul Goldschmidt, Nolan Arenado, Manny Machado, Giancarlo Stanton, Andrew McCutchen, Carlos Santana, Bryce Harper, Salvador Perez, Mike Trout and Eugenio Suárez.
The home run was Ramírez’s first since Aug. 30 and just his 12th this season. He entered Friday with an uncharacteristic .683 OPS in 117 games, in an injury-impacted campaign after he missed five weeks following left hamate surgery.
Ramírez has been dealt with the effects of that procedure since he came off the injured list on July 22. On Friday, he reminded us he’s always just one swing away from impacting a game in a big way.

The New York Yankees are out West on Friday night to begin a weekend series with the Arizona Diamondbacks.
Ahead of the matchup, New York received some bad news as superstar Aaron Judge heads back to the IL with a calf strain. Yankees manager Aaron Boone also made a few notable changes to his starting lineup for the series opener.
Yankees Announce Paul Goldschmidt Decision
After spending pretty much the entire season in a platoon role and not starting the last time the Yankees played on Wednesday, veteran slugger Paul Goldschmidt is in the lineup Friday, starting at first base and batting leadoff.
He’ll bat in front of Cody Bellinger, Heliot Ramos, and Ben Rice, who will move into the cleanup spot.
Here’s the full Yankees lineup:
Via Underdog MLB: “Yankees 9/18 P. Goldschmidt 1B C. Bellinger LF H. Ramos RF B. Rice DH A. Rosario 3B S. Jones CF G. Lombard Jr. SS A. Wells C A. Volpe 2B G. Cole SP.”
Yankees 9/18
P. Goldschmidt 1B
C. Bellinger LF
H. Ramos RF
B. Rice DH
A. Rosario 3B
S. Jones CF
G. Lombard Jr. SS
A. Wells C
A. Volpe 2B
G. Cole SP
— Underdog MLB (@UnderdogMLB) September 18, 2026
Goldschmidt’s 2026 Season
In his 16th MLB season and his second as a member of the Yankees, Goldschmidt has appeared in 101 games for New York, and across 332 at-bats, he’s hitting .253 with 42 runs, 84 hits, 18 home runs, and 50 RBIs while slugging .458 and maintaining a .773 OPS.
Looking at the Yankees
New York enters Friday’s contest with the D-backs holding an 88-64 overall record. They sit 5.0 games back of the Tampa Bay Rays for the AL East division lead and the No. 1 overall seed in the American League.
Currently, the Yankees hold the top Wild Card spot, and if the season ended today, they’d host a best-of-three series at Yankee Stadium in the Bronx against, coincidentally enough, the Boston Red Sox in what would mark a rematch of the 2025 postseason.

item.content:encoded:
Many fans rely on numbers to tell the story of a baseball season. For 2026, I’m going with letters. Here’s the story of the regular season from A to Z.

A: Yordan Alvarez: He’s the only qualifier in baseball with an OBP of over .400. He’s leading the American League in batting, on-base, slugging, OPS, and walks. Where would Joe Espada’s Astros be without him? Yordan is still the favorite to win the American League MVP, despite his numbers falling off a bit down the stretch.
B: Bryan Baker: Tampa Bay scored 698 runs and allowed 618 in games through September 17. That would give them a record of 84-68 according to the Pythagorean Theorem. But they were 93-59, nine games better. Credit in part goes to their closer Baker, leading the league with 40 saves this season..
C: Pete Crow-Armstrong: When the Cubs suffered through a 10-game losing streak in May, Pete batted just .161 (5-36 AB) in those 10 games. In games through September 17, PCA in 85 Cubs victories: .357/.442/.740. He scored 89 runs in 85 Cubs wins. The NL MVP by a mile. You cannot tell the story of the 2026 season without talking about Pete Crow-Armstrong.
D: Jacob deGrom: On September 10, deGrom started against the Mariners in Seattle. In six innings, he faced just 19 batters, one over the minimum. He struck out 12, gave up one hit, walked none, and didn’t allow a run. He left the game with Texas leading by three runs. The bullpen flushed away the lead and Texas wound up losing the game. The story of deGrom’s career. Jacob is historically significant. He has started 277 games in his career, and three of his top 10 (ranked by Pitchers’ Game Score) have come in 2026.
E: Errors: There’s only been one season EVER with fewer errors per game than 2026. Of course, that would be 2025. No pitcher has made more than four errors this season. In 1969, Jim Kaat won a Gold Glove, despite making eight errors (tied for the MLB lead with Boston’s Ray Culp among pitchers). Gold Gloves were all reputation in those days. In fact, Kaat’s longtime Minnesota teammate, Zoilo Versalles, won a Gold Glove in 1965 despite making 39 errors!
F: Freddie Freeman: Freeman has hit 32 doubles this year and 579 in his career. Is 579 doubles a lot? Well, that’s 90 more than the next-closest active player, Paul Goldschmidt. And when Freddie legs out his 600th, he’ll become only the 19th player with at least 600 doubles. He’s a little more than a season away from passing both Hank Aaron (624) and Barry Bonds (601).
G: Vladimir Guerrero Jr.: Vlad Jr. hit a home run every 25 at-bats in 2025. He’s hit a home run every 58 at-bats in 2026. He didn’t hit his first home run at home this year until Toronto’s 75th home game. He had gone 84 straight home games without a homer.
H: Bryce Harper: In March, Harper hit a two-run game-tying homer in the 8th inning of the WBC Finals. This season, his wRC+ (139) has been one of the top dozen in the majors. In October, can he lead the Phillies to his first World Series championship?
I: Raisel Iglesias: The Braves have spent all season in first place, and Iglesias is a big part of that. In the last 10 years (2017-2026) only one player (Kenley Jansen) has more saves than Iglesias. He’s 33-for-36 in save chances this year for the Braves. But here’s the thing: over the last five years, he’s saved 130 games for the Braves, but only one in the postseason. That has to change.
J: Aaron Judge: #99 missed 99 days (84 games) this season with a rib injury, but the three-time MVP came back in mid-September with enough time to get his timing back at the plate. Yankees fans will have to hope that the leg tightness isn’t a big deal.
K: Steven Kwan: There hasn’t been a hotter hitter in the American League since the start of July. Kwan is batting .350 since July 1, and .351 since the All-Star break. The Guardians have needed every bit of his offense, as José Ramírez has not been the same since returning from his broken left hamate bone.
L: Brandon Lowe: In his first season with Pittsburgh, Lowe has hit a career best 30 homers and has an OPS over .800. The Pirates offense was one of the big stories of the first half of the 2026 season, and Lowe was a big reason why. In the second half, injuries to Oneil Cruz and Ryan O’Hearn have sunk the Bucs but the offense was fun while it lasted.
M: Jacob Misiorowski: Milwaukee has the best record in baseball, and he’s a big reason why. Has any Brewers pitcher ever had a better season than the 24-year-old ace? Sorry, fans of Teddy Higuera. The answer is no. “The Miz” leads the majors in strikeouts (243). He leads the majors in ERA (1.89). He’s striking out more than 13 batters per nine innings! Misiorowski has had 1,053 pitches this season over 100.0 mph. No one else in pitch tracking era (2008-present) has had a season of 1,000 or more.
N: No-Hitters: On May 25, three Astros pitchers Tatsuya Imai (6 IP), Steven Okert (1 IP), and Alimber Santa (2 IP) combined to complete the Astros’ fifth combined no-hitter in franchise history. No one pitcher has completed a no-hitter since Blake Snell did it in August of 2024 for the Giants.
O: Shohei Ohtani: There are two players whose last name starts with “O” with more homers than Ohtani this season: Matt Olson and Kazuma Okamoto. But Ohtani made 14 brilliant starts (1.79 ERA) and his wRC+ of 142 is in the top 10 in the game.
P: Salvador Perez: The 36-year-old put up nearly 600 at-bats this season. And while most of them came as a DH or 1B, he did start 44 games behind the plate. In his 15-year career, he’s caught 1,427 games (1,396 starts) and nearly 12,000 innings.
Q: Quick games: On September 7, in an afternoon game at Citizens Bank Park, the Phillies beat the Braves 1-0 in a game that took 1:51 to play. On June 16 at Dodger Stadium, the Dodgers defeated the Rays 1-0 in a game that took 1:52 to complete. And in early April, the Royals defeated the White Sox in games on April 10 and 11 that lasted in 1:54 and 1:55, respectively. Thank you, pitch clock.
R: Eduardo Rodriguez: The Diamondbacks have won 22 of E-Rod’s first 30 starts. Talk about valuable! He has a 2.62 ERA this season (it was 5.04 and 5.02 in the two previous seasons). This is his best year since 2019.
S: Cam Schlittler: Is he the AL MVP, or just the AL Cy Young? The Yankees won 20 of his 31 starts. The Yankees don’t need a lot of offense when he takes the mound. He has a 1.14 ERA in 16 road starts this season! Since earned runs became official in both leagues in 1913, Schlittler’s 1.14 road ERA is the fourth best (minimum 15 road starts). The top three: Bob Gibson in 1968 (0.81 ERA); Walter Johnson in 1913 (1.06 ERA); and Greg Maddux in 1995 (1.12 ERA).
T: Bruce Turang: What a player! His OPS has gone up in each of his first four seasons. He’s now a 20 HR/20 SB/100 runs/100 RBI player. The Brewers need him to improve his performance in last year’s NLCS vs. the Dodgers, when he went 1-for-15 (.067).
U: Uncle Charlie (curveball): The curveball is heading toward extinction, much like individual no-hitters. Curveballs have only accounted for 6.4% of pitches this season, the second lowest rate since first tracked in 2008 (2024: 6.1%). That’s pure curves, not including slow curves or knuckle-curves. Want to know which pitcher has thrown the most curveballs (including knuckle and slow curves) this year? Philadelphia’s Aaron Nola, at 942.
V: Miguel Vargas: The White Sox have been one of the best stories this year, and we could have given the “V” to manager Max Venable. But Vargas’ 31 home runs and stealing 19 bases in 21 attempts makes him the choice. Vargas has a 4.7 WAR this season, up from 1.9 last year.
W: Willson and Wilyer, the heart of the Boston lineup. Right fielder Wilyer Abreu leads the American League with 36 doubles. He also leads the AL in outfield assists with 12. Willson Contreras has an OPS of .905, second in AL to Alvarez, even ahead of Rays slugger Junior Caminero. Remember, Boston was 14 games under .500 as late as June 24. And then the season turned around.
X: Xander Bogaerts: The Padres have played well down the stretch and now appear likely to reach the postseason. And X-Man has contributed, stealing 21 bases in 22 attempts this year. It’s no fluke, either. He stole 20 of 22 last season. In his four seasons with the Padres, he has stolen 73 bases in 81 attempts. That’s efficiency.
Y: Yoshinobu Yamamoto: The Dodgers’ Yoshinobu Yamamoto has a 1.98 ERA in 10 starts after the All-Star break. He’s probably the key to the Dodgers’ chances of completing a three-peat. Who can forget what he did last October, when he went 5-1, with a 1.45 ERA in 37.1 postseason innings.
Z: Zack Wheeler: From July 21 through August 24, Wheeler had a stretch of seven starts that saw him give up 26 runs (25 earned) in 31.1 innings (7.18 ERA). He was terrific in the first half and recaptured his form down the stretch. If the Phillies are going to go deep into October, they’ll need Wheeler (and their other two aces) to be at the top of their game.
Editors’ Note: Elliott Kalb - dubbed “Mr. Stats” decades ago by Marv Albert and Bob Costas - is the former Senior Editorial Director at MLB Network and a longtime contributor of research and information to NBC Sports’ telecasts.
